knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

## EDA Objective
Start EDA with the distribution of the target variable, `y`, and then move on to the distribution of the predictors. Inspect dataset for missing values and outliers. Preview correlation between the predictors and the target variable.

## Ingest
EDA is on the `bank-additional-full.csv` dataset, which contains all examples, ordered by date (from May 2008 to November 2010). The dataset has 41,188 rows and 21 columns. The target variable is `y`, which indicates whether the client subscribed to a term deposit. The predictors include both numerical and categorical variables, such as age, job, marital status, education, default, balance, housing loan, personal loan, contact communication type, day of the week, month of contact, duration of the call, number of contacts performed during this campaign and for this client (numeric), number of days since the client was last contacted from a previous campaign (numeric), number of contacts performed before this campaign and for this client (numeric), outcome of the previous marketing campaign (categorical), employment variation rate (numeric), consumer price index (numeric), consumer confidence index (numeric), euribor 3 month rate (numeric), and number of employees (numeric).
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

bank_add <- read.csv("../Data/bank-additional-full.csv", sep = ";")
# bank_full <- read.csv("../Data/bank-full.csv", sep = ";")
```


## Distribution of Response
The distribution of the response variable `y` is shown below. The majority of the observations are "no" (not subscribed), with a smaller proportion of "yes" (subscribed). This indicates that the dataset is imbalanced, which may affect the performance of predictive models.
```{r}
# Distribution of y
table(bank_add$y)
ggplot(bank_add, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_bar() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Target Variable", x = "Target", y = "Count")
```

## Distributions of Numerical Predictors
```{r}
# Identify numerical predictors
num_vars <- bank_add %>%
  select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  names()

# Convert to long format for faceting
bank_long <- bank_add %>%
  select(all_of(num_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

# Plot distributions
ggplot(bank_long, aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Numerical Predictors",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Frequency"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## Five Number Summary of Numerical Predictors
```{r}
# Create a five-number summary table for all numerical predictors
five_num_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable = num_vars,
  t(sapply(bank_add[num_vars], fivenum))
)

# Rename columns
colnames(five_num_summary) <- c(
  "Variable", "Min", "Q1", "Median", "Q3", "Max"
)

# Display as a formatted table
knitr::kable(
  five_num_summary,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Five-Number Summary of Numerical Predictors"
)
```

## Density Plots by Subscription Status
Density Plots grouped by subscription status (`y`) for each numerical predictor. This will help visualize how the distributions differ between those who subscribed and those who did not. The predictors that show potential differences in distribution between the two groups may be more informative for predictive modeling: cons.conf.idx, cons.price.idx, emp.var.rate, euribor3m, nr.employed.
```{r}
bank_long <- bank_add %>%
  select(all_of(num_vars), y) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(num_vars),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Value"
  )

ggplot(bank_long, aes(x = Value, fill = y)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Predictor Distributions by Subscription Status",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Subscribed"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```


## Faceted Bar Charts for Categorical Predictors
Faceted bar charts for categorical predictors: notice that many predictors have 'unknown' as a category, which may need to be addressed in the cleaning process.

Also notice pdays, which is a numeric predictor but has a large number of 999 values, indicating that the client was not previously contacted. This may need to be treated as a categorical variable or imputed in some way.
```{r}
# Identify categorical predictors
cat_vars <- bank_add %>%
  select(where(~ is.factor(.) | is.character(.))) %>%
  select(-any_of("y")) %>%
  names()

# Convert to long format
bank_cat_long <- bank_add %>%
  select(all_of(cat_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Category"
  )

# Plot categorical predictor distributions
ggplot(bank_cat_long, aes(x = Category)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of Categorical Predictors",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 45,
      hjust = 1
    ),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```


## Boxplots to examine outliers
Balance, campaign, duration, pdays, and previous are all heavily right-skewed, with many outliers. The boxplots below show the distribution of these numerical predictors by subscription status (`y`).

Important note: the duration attribute highly affects the output target (e.g., if duration=0 then y="no"). Yet, the duration is not known before a call is performed. Also, after the end of the call y is obviously known. Thus, this input should **only be included for benchmark purposes** and should be discarded if the intention is to have a realistic predictive model.
```{r}
ggplot(bank_long, aes(x = y, y = Value, fill = y)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Predictor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Numerical Predictors by Subscription Status",
    x = "Subscribed",
    y = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## Missing or Unknown Values
There are no missing values in the dataset. However, **default, education, housing, loan, job, and marital** have "unknown" values. The table below shows the proportion of unknown values for each predictor. This will help identify which predictors may need to be cleaned or imputed.

```{r}
# look for missing values in the dataset
sum(is.na(bank_add))

# look for unknown values in the dataset
sum(bank_add == "unknown") / sum(bank_add != "unknown")

# breakdown the proportion of unknown values by predictor
unknown_summary <- bank_add %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(. == "unknown") / n())) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Predictor",
    values_to = "Proportion_Unknown"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Proportion_Unknown))

# Display results
knitr::kable(
  unknown_summary,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Proportion of Unknown Values by Predictor"
)
```
